adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Every autumn my grandmother cleared the kitchen table, tied on her apron, and announced that the season of baking had begun. She had grown up in a mill town, the eldest of six children, and she learned to cook from her mother, who measured nothing and remembered everything. The recipes she passed down were written on index cards in a cramped hand, stained with butter and vanilla, and many of them carried notes in the margins about the weather, the temperament of the oven, and the moods of children.

The first thing she taught me was patience. Butter had to soften on its own, and the microwave was forbidden. Flour had to be sifted twice, not once, because the grind she remembered was coarser than anything we could buy in a supermarket. One card, in her mother's hand, said only: good for a rainy Sunday, and for anyone who arrives without warning. She would hold a handful of flour up to the window and let it fall through her fingers, watching how it drifted, and only then would she decide whether the dough needed another spoonful of water. That habit, she said, came from her own mother, who had baked through wars and a flood and a winter when the river froze solid enough for trucks to cross.

Her kitchen smelled of cinnamon and scorched sugar from October through December. Neighbours dropped by without warning and she fed every one of them. The minister came on Tuesdays. The mail carrier came whenever the snow allowed. Children came after school, pretending to help, mostly hoping for the bowl and the spoon.

The dough itself was simple: butter, sugar, an egg, flour, a pinch of salt, and a little vanilla. She creamed the butter and the sugar until the mixture turned pale and fluffy, then beat in the egg, then folded the dry ingredients through with a wooden spoon. The dough rested in the refrigerator for an hour, wrapped in waxed paper, while she told stories about her brothers and the town as it used to be.

When the dough was ready she rolled it out on a floured board, cut it into shapes with a tin cutter shaped like a star, and set the pieces on a greased tray, leaving room between them because they spread in the heat. Bake at 350 degrees for 25 minutes, until the edges turn golden, then cool them on a wire rack before decorating.

The decorating was my job. She mixed powdered sugar with a few drops of milk and a drop of food colouring, and we painted the stars and the bells and the trees with small brushes. Most of my cookies ended up with far too much icing. She never complained. She would set them on a plate, cover the plate with a clean cloth, and put it in the pantry for the visitors who would surely arrive before the week was out.

Years later I found her recipe box in a cupboard, and the cards still smelled faintly of vanilla. I have tried to reproduce those afternoons, and I have never quite managed it. The cookies are good, but the kitchen is too quiet, and nobody drops by without warning anymore.
